source: Linear Momentum
Momentum p = mv is a vector, and a system's momentum is the vector sum of its parts.
Students add momenta as plain numbers, forgetting that opposite directions cancel.

In Physical Science you met momentum as mass times velocity. Physics 1 adds one important idea: momentum is a vector. It points the way the object moves, so on a line it carries a sign, and in a plane it has components, just like the vectors you add by components.

Momentum is $\role{momentum}{\vec{p}} = \role{mass}{m}\role{velocity}{\vec{v}}$, measured in $\text{kg·m/s}$. On a line, pick a positive direction and give each momentum a sign. The momentum of a system is the vector sum of the momenta of its parts: $\vec{p}_{\text{tot}} = m_1\vec{v}_1 + m_2\vec{v}_2 + \dots$

Why multiply mass by velocity? Because that product is what a force changes. Newton's second law says $F = ma = m\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$, so $F\Delta t = \Delta(mv)$: a push lasting a while changes $mv$, whatever the mass. A loaded truck and a bicycle at the same speed are very different to stop, and $mv$ measures exactly that difference. Since velocity has a direction, so does $mv$, and two momenta in opposite directions cancel when you add them.
Momentum bars for two gliders: each bar is $mv$ with a sign, and the teal bar is the total.
Worked examples
A $1200\ \text{kg}$ car drives west at $15\ \text{m/s}$. Taking east as positive, find its momentum.
One object, with a sign
$p = -1.8 \times 10^{4}\ \text{kg·m/s}$
West is the negative direction, so $v = -15\ \text{m/s}$.
The size is $18{,}000\ \text{kg·m/s}$; the minus sign says "west".
Cart A ($2.0\ \text{kg}$) moves right at $3.0\ \text{m/s}$. Cart B ($4.0\ \text{kg}$) moves left at $1.0\ \text{m/s}$. Find the total momentum (right is positive).
Two objects on a line
$+2.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$
$p_{\text{tot}} = 6.0 + (-4.0) = +2.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$, pointing right.
On ice, puck 1 ($0.20\ \text{kg}$) slides east at $6.0\ \text{m/s}$ and puck 2 ($0.20\ \text{kg}$) slides north at $8.0\ \text{m/s}$. How big is their total momentum?
Two objects at right angles
$2.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$
East component: $p_x = (0.20)(6.0) = 1.2\ \text{kg·m/s}$. North component: $p_y = (0.20)(8.0) = 1.6\ \text{kg·m/s}$.
$|\vec{p}| = \sqrt{1.2^2 + 1.6^2} = 2.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$, pointing $53^\circ$ north of east.
Adding the sizes ($2.8$) would be wrong because the momenta are not in the same direction.

Adding momenta as plain numbers. Two $3\ \text{kg·m/s}$ momenta can total $6$, $0$ or anything in between, depending on their directions. Before you add, write every velocity with its sign (or split it into components). Quick check: if two objects move toward each other, the total must be smaller than the bigger of the two momenta.

A small, fast object can carry as much momentum as a big, slow one: a $0.15\ \text{kg}$ baseball at $40\ \text{m/s}$ and a $6.0\ \text{kg}$ bowling ball at $1.0\ \text{m/s}$ both have $6.0\ \text{kg·m/s}$. Try collisions with momentum bars in the Momentum and Collisions lab of the Science Lab.
